questions.questionText: TerramEarth is migrating a massive Hadoop cluster to Cloud Dataproc to run daily Spark data aggregation jobs. To optimize costs, they want to heavily utilize Spot VMs. Which Dataproc architectural configuration properly handles compute volatility without risking HDFS data loss or job failure?
options: Provision the Master node as a Standard VM, and provision both Primary Workers and Secondary Workers as Spot VMs.
Provision the Master and Primary Workers as Standard VMs, and provision Secondary Workers as Spot VMs, ensuring HDFS is disabled on Secondary Workers.
Provision the Master node as a Spot VM with a persistent disk, and allocate all worker nodes as Standard VMs to ensure data durability.
Provision the entire cluster (Master, Primary, and Secondary Workers) as Spot VMs and enable Dataproc Auto-scaling to recover preempted nodes rapidly.
correctAnswers: Provision the Master and Primary Workers as Standard VMs, and provision Secondary Workers as Spot VMs, ensuring HDFS is disabled on Secondary Workers.

explanation.general explanation: In Dataproc, Primary Workers store HDFS data and process compute, while Secondary Workers only process compute and do not store HDFS data. Because Spot VMs can be preempted at any time, using them for Primary Workers would lead to HDFS block loss and cluster corruption. Therefore, Spot VMs must only be used for Secondary Workers, with Master and Primary nodes running on Standard VMs.

why other options are wrong.Provision the Master node as a Standard: Using Spot VMs for Primary Workers is highly dangerous because they hold HDFS data. Preemption will cause data loss and job failures.
why other options are wrong.Provision the Master node as a Spot VM w: The Master node manages the cluster state (YARN resource manager, HDFS NameNode). If the Master node is preempted, the entire cluster fails immediately.
why other options are wrong.Provision the entire cluster (Master, Pr: An all-Spot cluster is highly unstable. Preemption of the master or primary workers will destroy the cluster and lose data before auto-scaling can respond.

questions.questionText: You are deploying a critical background processing service on Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE). To save costs, you created a dedicated Spot node pool for these workers. However, you want to ensure that your mission-critical frontend web pods are never scheduled on these Spot nodes. Which GKE mechanism automatically prevents this when a Spot node pool is created?
options: GKE automatically applies the `cloud.google.com/gke-spot=true:NoSchedule` taint to Spot nodes, requiring pods to have a specific toleration to be scheduled there.
GKE forces Spot node pools to run in a separate VPC subnet that standard pods cannot route traffic to.
Spot nodes in GKE natively reject all Deployments unless they are explicitly wrapped in a SpotWorkload custom resource definition.
GKE assigns a lower PriorityClass to Spot nodes, ensuring standard pods always preempt Spot workloads.
correctAnswers: GKE automatically applies the `cloud.google.com/gke-spot=true:NoSchedule` taint to Spot nodes, requiring pods to have a specific toleration to be scheduled there.

explanation.general explanation: When you create a node pool using Spot VMs in GKE, Google automatically applies the `cloud.google.com/gke-spot=true:NoSchedule` taint to those nodes. This ensures that standard workloads are not accidentally scheduled on volatile hardware. You must explicitly add a matching toleration to your worker pods for them to run on the Spot nodes.

why other options are wrong.GKE forces Spot node pools to run in a s: Spot nodes share the same VPC subnets and networking as standard nodes in the cluster.
why other options are wrong.Spot nodes in GKE natively reject all De: There is no 'SpotWorkload' CRD requirement. Native Kubernetes tolerations and nodeSelectors are used.
why other options are wrong.GKE assigns a lower PriorityClass to Spo: PriorityClasses are assigned to Pods, not Nodes, and dictate Pod-to-Pod preemption for scheduling, not underlying infrastructure volatility.

questions.questionText: Your e-commerce backend requires a baseline of 50 Standard VMs to guarantee handling of baseline traffic. During sales events, you want to dynamically scale up to an additional 200 instances using Spot VMs to minimize costs. Which Compute Engine architecture is required to achieve this mixed compute volatility configuration natively?
options: Create a single Managed Instance Group (MIG) with a Standard Instance Template. Set the autoscaler's `scaleOutProfile` to 'SPOT_ONLY'.

Create two separate Managed Instance Groups (MIGs): one using a Standard instance template and one using a Spot instance template. Attach both MIGs as backends to the same Backend Service in your Load Balancer.
Configure a single MIG with an Instance Template configured for Spot VMs, but apply a Stateful Policy to the first 50 instances to prevent them from being preempted.
Use a Regional MIG and configure the `mixedInstancesPolicy` to maintain a 20% Standard and 80% Spot distribution target.
correctAnswers: Create two separate Managed Instance Groups (MIGs): one using a Standard instance template and one using a Spot instance template. Attach both MIGs as backends to the same Backend Service in your Load Balancer.

explanation.general explanation: Compute Engine Managed Instance Groups (MIGs) dictate their instance type and provisioning model strictly through the attached Instance Template. A single MIG cannot natively mix Standard and Spot VMs via a distribution policy (unlike AWS ASGs). To achieve a guaranteed baseline of Standard VMs and scale out using Spot VMs, you must create two separate MIGs and attach them both to the same Load Balancer backend service.

why other options are wrong.Create a single Managed Instance Group (: There is no 'scaleOutProfile' setting in GCP MIG autoscalers that switches the provisioning model dynamically.
why other options are wrong.Configure a single MIG with an Instance: Stateful Policies protect data disks and IPs during recreation; they cannot magically convert a Spot VM into a non-preemptible Standard VM.
why other options are wrong.Use a Regional MIG and configure the `mi: GCP MIGs do not currently support a native `mixedInstancesPolicy` for blending Spot and Standard instances within a single group.

questions.questionText: You are processing 5-minute video chunks on Spot VMs. Preemptions frequently cause chunks to be lost right before completion, forcing a full retry. How should you architect the application to gracefully handle Spot VM volatility and save the intermediate encoding progress?
options: Use a Compute Engine startup script to monitor the `compute.googleapis.com/instance/preemptions` metric and pause the encoding process when the metric spikes.
Implement a shutdown script on the VM that captures the OS-level ACPI G2 Soft Off signal, flushes the intermediate encoding buffer to Cloud Storage, and gracefully exits within 30 seconds.
Configure the Spot VM with a 'Suspend' preemption action instead of 'Delete', ensuring the VM automatically pauses the video encoding without any application-level changes.
Set the `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` to 300 on the VM instance template to allow the 5-minute chunk to complete before Google forces the preemption.
correctAnswers: Implement a shutdown script on the VM that captures the OS-level ACPI G2 Soft Off signal, flushes the intermediate encoding buffer to Cloud Storage, and gracefully exits within 30 seconds.

explanation.general explanation: When Compute Engine preempts a Spot VM, it sends an ACPI G2 Soft Off signal to the guest OS. You have a maximum of 30 seconds to run a shutdown script before the instance is forcibly terminated. Capturing this signal allows you to gracefully flush intermediate states/buffers to persistent storage (like Cloud Storage) within that 30-second window, preventing the loss of work.

why other options are wrong.Use a Compute Engine startup script to m: Metrics are aggregated and delayed. They cannot be used for real-time interception of an impending preemption on a specific instance.
why other options are wrong.Configure the Spot VM with a 'Suspend' p: While suspending Spot VMs is possible under certain constraints, application-level checkpointing is vastly more reliable for video encoding because Spot suspend requires specific machine families and capacity guarantees that might not be met, resulting in termination anyway.
why other options are wrong.Set the `terminationGracePeriodSeconds`: `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` is a Kubernetes (GKE) concept, not a Compute Engine instance template property. Furthermore, Spot VMs enforce a hard 30-second preemption limit regardless.

questions.questionText: Your data science team uses Vertex AI Custom Training jobs. To reduce training costs for deep learning models that take 48 hours to complete, they want to utilize Spot VMs for the worker pools. What is a critical requirement for their training code to succeed in this volatile environment?
options: The training code must be wrapped in a Docker container that exposes an HTTP endpoint for Vertex AI to send a REST payload before preemption.
The training code must frequently write checkpoints to Cloud Storage and be designed to automatically load the latest checkpoint upon restart.
The training code must use a shared NFS volume (Filestore) to store in-memory tensors, as Vertex AI automatically re-attaches Filestore to new Spot instances.
The training code must be split into execution graphs that strictly finish within the 24-hour Spot VM maximum runtime limit.
correctAnswers: The training code must frequently write checkpoints to Cloud Storage and be designed to automatically load the latest checkpoint upon restart.

explanation.general explanation: When using Spot VMs for Vertex AI Custom Training, preemptions are highly likely over a 48-hour period. Vertex AI handles the underlying infrastructure by automatically provisioning a replacement Spot VM when one is preempted. However, the application must handle the state. The training code must implement checkpointing (saving model weights periodically to Cloud Storage) and must automatically detect and resume from the latest checkpoint when the script restarts on the new VM.

why other options are wrong.The training code must be wrapped in a D: Vertex AI does not send a REST payload before preemption. The VM simply receives standard OS termination signals.
why other options are wrong.The training code must use a shared NFS: While possible, Cloud Storage is the standard, native, and cost-effective method for ML checkpointing in Vertex AI. Managing Filestore for ephemeral training workers is an anti-pattern.
why other options are wrong.The training code must be split into exe: Spot VMs do not have a 24-hour maximum runtime limit (unlike legacy Preemptible VMs). They can run indefinitely until preempted.

questions.questionText: You are migrating a legacy computational workload to Google Cloud. The workload scripts were originally designed to run on legacy Preemptible VMs, and they implement complex logic to forcefully restart themselves precisely every 23 hours to avoid sudden data loss. You plan to use the newer Spot VMs provisioning model. How does this impact the legacy restart logic?
options: Spot VMs enforce a 12-hour maximum runtime, so the restart logic must be aggressively updated to run twice as often.
Spot VMs do not have a maximum runtime limit; they only terminate when Compute Engine requires the capacity, so the 23-hour forced restart logic is unnecessary and can be removed.
Spot VMs utilize the same strict 24-hour hard limit as legacy Preemptible VMs, so the legacy restart logic must be maintained exactly as is.
Spot VMs automatically snapshot their memory to persistent disk at the 24-hour mark, eliminating the need for application-level restart logic.
correctAnswers: Spot VMs do not have a maximum runtime limit; they only terminate when Compute Engine requires the capacity, so the 23-hour forced restart logic is unnecessary and can be removed.

explanation.general explanation: A key difference between the older legacy Preemptible VMs and the modern Spot VMs is the maximum runtime. Preemptible VMs have a hard system-enforced termination at 24 hours. Spot VMs do not have any maximum runtime limit. They will run indefinitely until Google Cloud needs the compute capacity. Therefore, custom scripts designed to preemptively restart at 23 hours are unnecessary and should be removed.

why other options are wrong.Spot VMs enforce a 12-hour maximum runti: Spot VMs have no maximum runtime limit.
why other options are wrong.Spot VMs utilize the same strict 24-hour: This is factually incorrect; Spot VMs explicitly removed the 24-hour constraint.
why other options are wrong.Spot VMs automatically snapshot their me: Spot VMs do not automatically snapshot memory. If preempted, they terminate or stop based on configuration, but state management is up to the user.

questions.questionText: Your engineering team deploys containerized microservices using GKE Autopilot to completely offload node management. They want to utilize Spot compute to drastically reduce the cost of a stateless analytics microservice. How should you correctly configure compute volatility for this service in GKE Autopilot?
options: Use gcloud to create a secondary Autopilot cluster dedicated entirely to Spot compute.
In the pod specification YAML, add the `nodeSelector` with the key-value pair `cloud.google.com/gke-spot: "true"`.
Configure a custom Kubernetes `StorageClass` with the provisioner set to `spot.gke.io` and mount it to the analytics pod.
Modify the Autopilot cluster's default NodePool settings in the Google Cloud Console to enable Spot pricing.
correctAnswers: In the pod specification YAML, add the `nodeSelector` with the key-value pair `cloud.google.com/gke-spot: "true"`.

explanation.general explanation: In GKE Autopilot, you do not manage nodes or node pools directly. To run workloads on Spot compute, you simply specify the requirement at the Pod level using a `nodeSelector`. By adding `cloud.google.com/gke-spot: "true"` to your pod spec, GKE Autopilot automatically provisions Spot capacity on the backend and schedules the pod onto it, seamlessly managing the volatility.

why other options are wrong.Use gcloud to create a secondary Autopil: Autopilot clusters are not strictly 'spot' or 'standard'. The cluster dynamically provisions capacity based on the pod specifications submitted.
why other options are wrong.Configure a custom Kubernetes `StorageCl: StorageClasses manage persistent volumes, not compute node provisioning.
why other options are wrong.Modify the Autopilot cluster's default N: You cannot manage NodePools in GKE Autopilot; node management is entirely abstracted away.

questions.questionText: You configured a high-performance Spot VM with 4 attached Local SSDs to act as an ephemeral cache for complex rendering tasks. The workload runs for days, caching heavy assets locally. The instance is suddenly preempted by Compute Engine. You immediately restart the instance. What is the state of the data on the Local SSDs?
options: The data is perfectly retained because the instance was stopped and restarted within the same zone.
The data is permanently lost. Upon preemption, Local SSDs are completely wiped and cannot be recovered.
The data is preserved only if the preemption action was configured to 'STOP' instead of 'DELETE'.
The data is temporarily backed up to a hidden Cloud Storage bucket and will be transparently restored upon boot.
correctAnswers: The data is permanently lost. Upon preemption, Local SSDs are completely wiped and cannot be recovered.

explanation.general explanation: Local SSDs are physically attached to the host server where the VM runs. When a Spot VM is preempted (regardless of whether it is configured to STOP or DELETE), the VM is removed from the host hardware. Consequently, any data on the attached Local SSDs is irrevocably lost. You must design Spot VM workloads to treat Local SSDs as strictly volatile scratch space.

why other options are wrong.The data is perfectly retained because t: When stopped, the VM loses its association with the physical host, meaning the Local SSD is lost.
why other options are wrong.The data is preserved only if the preemp: Configuring the preemption action to STOP preserves the *Persistent Disk* (the boot disk or attached PDs), but it does not preserve Local SSDs.
why other options are wrong.The data is temporarily backed up to a h: GCP does not automatically backup or restore Local SSD data. It is ephemeral by definition.

questions.questionText: Your team executes nightly Dataflow batch jobs that parse terabytes of non-time-sensitive log data. The pipeline is heavily bound by compute costs. You want to utilize Spot VMs to minimize costs while ensuring the job still guarantees completion by the morning. Which two configurations should you apply to the Dataflow pipeline? (Choose two)
options: Set the worker machine type to a Preemptible VM class explicitly in the pipeline options.
Enable Flexible Resource Scheduling (FlexRS) by passing the parameter `--flexRSGoal=COST_OPTIMIZED`.
Configure the pipeline to write intermediate PCollection states to a multi-region Cloud Storage bucket manually.
Ensure the Dataflow job is submitted as a Batch job, as FlexRS is not supported for Streaming jobs.
Disable Dataflow Shuffle to prevent data loss when Spot worker nodes are preempted.
correctAnswers: Enable Flexible Resource Scheduling (FlexRS) by passing the parameter `--flexRSGoal=COST_OPTIMIZED`.
Ensure the Dataflow job is submitted as a Batch job, as FlexRS is not supported for Streaming jobs.

explanation.general explanation: Dataflow Flexible Resource Scheduling (FlexRS) is designed specifically to reduce batch processing costs by utilizing a mix of standard and preemptible (Spot) VMs. It delays job execution to find the optimal time to grab cheap compute capacity, guaranteeing execution within a 6-hour window. FlexRS is only applicable to Batch jobs, not Streaming jobs.

why other options are wrong.Set the worker machine type to a Preempt: While you can manually set workers to preemptible, using FlexRS is the native, managed way to guarantee completion within a timeframe while optimizing for Spot pricing without manual intervention.
why other options are wrong.Configure the pipeline to write intermed: Dataflow automatically handles state and checkpointing when using FlexRS and Dataflow Shuffle. You do not need to manually write intermediate PCollections to GCS to survive preemptions.
why other options are wrong.Disable Dataflow Shuffle to prevent data: You should actually *enable* (or rely on the default) Dataflow Shuffle. FlexRS requires the Dataflow Shuffle service because it moves the shuffle state off the volatile worker VMs and into the Google-managed backend, protecting data during preemptions.

questions.questionText: You are deploying a graceful shutdown process for a long-running simulation pod on GKE. The pod specification sets `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` to 120 seconds. The deployment is scheduled on a Spot node pool. When Google Cloud decides to preempt the underlying Spot node, which two events will occur regarding your pod's lifecycle? (Choose two)
options: The pod will receive a `SIGTERM` signal, notifying the application to begin its graceful shutdown procedures.
The pod will be allowed to run for the full 120 seconds defined in `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` before the Spot node is terminated.
GKE will intercept the Spot preemption signal and automatically Live Migrate the pod to a Standard node to honor the 120-second grace period.
The pod will be sent a `SIGKILL` signal and forcefully terminated after approximately 25 seconds, regardless of the 120-second setting.
The pod will be suspended and its memory state saved to disk, bypassing the `SIGTERM` process entirely.
correctAnswers: The pod will receive a `SIGTERM` signal, notifying the application to begin its graceful shutdown procedures.
The pod will be sent a `SIGKILL` signal and forcefully terminated after approximately 25 seconds, regardless of the 120-second setting.

explanation.general explanation: Spot VMs provide a strict 30-second warning before termination. In GKE, when the kubelet detects the preemption notice on a Spot node, it begins gracefully terminating the pods (sending `SIGTERM`). However, because the underlying hardware will vanish in 30 seconds, GKE caps the graceful shutdown window for pods on Spot nodes to 25 seconds. After 25 seconds, a `SIGKILL` is issued, forcefully terminating the pod, even if the pod's `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` requested 120 seconds.

why other options are wrong.The pod will be allowed to run for the f: Hardware limits supersede Kubernetes software configurations. The hardware vanishes in 30 seconds, so the 120-second request is physically impossible to honor.
why other options are wrong.GKE will intercept the Spot preemption s: Spot VMs do not support Live Migration, and Kubernetes pods cannot be seamlessly live-migrated between nodes in this manner without a restart.
why other options are wrong.The pod will be suspended and its memory: GKE pods do not suspend memory state to disk natively upon node preemption; they are terminated.

questions.questionText: Helicopter Racing League (HRL) uses a Spot Managed Instance Group (MIG) as subscriber workers for a Pub/Sub queue containing video rendering tasks. The tasks take 5 minutes, so the Pub/Sub acknowledgment (ack) deadline is set to 10 minutes. If a Spot VM is preempted 1 minute into rendering, the task sits unacknowledged for 9 more minutes before Pub/Sub redelivers it, severely degrading pipeline throughput. How can you drastically reduce this redelivery delay caused by compute volatility?
options: Configure the Spot MIG to use an external HTTPS load balancer and set the backend timeout to 30 seconds.
Write a shutdown script on the Spot VMs that immediately sends a `NACK` (negative acknowledgment) to Pub/Sub or modifies the ack deadline to 0 for the active message before the instance terminates.
Switch the Pub/Sub subscription from Pull to Push, as Push subscriptions automatically detect Spot VM preemption and retry immediately.
Reduce the Pub/Sub ack deadline to 30 seconds, and configure the application to process the task faster.
correctAnswers: Write a shutdown script on the Spot VMs that immediately sends a `NACK` (negative acknowledgment) to Pub/Sub or modifies the ack deadline to 0 for the active message before the instance terminates.

explanation.general explanation: Spot VMs receive a 30-second ACPI termination warning. By catching this signal in a shutdown script, you can instruct your application to negatively acknowledge (NACK) the message or reset its ack deadline to 0. This tells Pub/Sub that the worker is abandoning the task, prompting Pub/Sub to instantly redeliver the message to a different, active worker, completely eliminating the 9-minute wait.

why other options are wrong.Configure the Spot MIG to use an externa: The workers are Pub/Sub subscribers pulling messages, not HTTP servers behind a load balancer receiving requests.
why other options are wrong.Switch the Pub/Sub subscription from Pul: Push subscriptions rely on HTTP responses. If the VM dies unexpectedly, the Push endpoint will simply time out based on the ack deadline. It does not automatically detect preemption any faster.
why other options are wrong.Reduce the Pub/Sub ack deadline to 30 se: The task intrinsically takes 5 minutes. Reducing the deadline to 30 seconds would cause Pub/Sub to constantly redeliver the message while the worker is still actively processing it, leading to massive duplicate processing.

questions.questionText: Mountkirk Games uses Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) and Agones to host dedicated multiplayer game servers globally. To reduce costs during off-peak hours, a junior engineer proposes migrating the primary `GameServer` node pools from Standard VMs to Spot VMs. Why is this an architectural anti-pattern for this specific workload?
options: Agones requires strict stateful disk attachments (Persistent Volumes) for high-speed logging, which are incompatible with Spot VMs.
Spot VMs can be preempted with only a 30-second warning, which forcefully disconnects active players mid-match, severely degrading the user experience.
GKE Spot node pools cannot be exposed via external UDP Load Balancers, which are required for real-time multiplayer gaming traffic.
Agones relies on Kubernetes daemonsets that are natively blocked from running on Spot nodes by the `cloud.google.com/gke-spot=true:NoSchedule` taint.
correctAnswers: Spot VMs can be preempted with only a 30-second warning, which forcefully disconnects active players mid-match, severely degrading the user experience.

explanation.general explanation: Dedicated game servers (like those managed by Agones) maintain long-lived, active UDP/TCP connections with clients. They are highly stateful in memory during a match. If a Spot node is preempted, the 30-second warning is insufficient to gracefully migrate active player connections to a new server without dropping them. Disconnecting players mid-match is unacceptable for gaming architectures. Spot VMs should only be used for stateless microservices (e.g., matchmaking, leaderboards).

why other options are wrong.Agones requires strict stateful disk att: Spot VMs fully support Persistent Volumes. However, statefulness in gaming is primarily in-memory and connection-based, not just disk-based.
why other options are wrong.GKE Spot node pools cannot be exposed vi: Spot nodes share the exact same networking capabilities as standard nodes; they can absolutely be exposed via UDP load balancers.
why other options are wrong.Agones relies on Kubernetes daemonsets t: While the taint exists, DaemonSets can simply be configured with the appropriate tolerations to run on Spot nodes. The real issue is the abrupt termination of player sessions.

questions.questionText: A financial institution runs quantitative risk models using a massively parallel grid compute architecture. They require 50,000 vCPUs globally. The workloads are stateless and extremely fault-tolerant. To maximize their budget, they want to utilize Spot VMs. Which operational strategy leverages the Spot provisioning model most effectively for this scale?
options: Deploy all 50,000 vCPUs in a single zone (e.g., `us-central1-a`) to maximize data locality and minimize inter-zone egress costs, relying on the fixed 91% Spot discount.
Distribute the workloads across multiple regions and zones programmatically based on real-time Spot pricing and capacity variations, as Spot discounts are dynamic.
Provision the grid using Preemptible VMs instead of Spot VMs to guarantee a flat, predictable 80% discount rate globally.
Commit to a 3-year Flexible Committed Use Discount (CUD) applied directly to the Spot VM fleets to lower the dynamic price floor further.
correctAnswers: Distribute the workloads across multiple regions and zones programmatically based on real-time Spot pricing and capacity variations, as Spot discounts are dynamic.

explanation.general explanation: Unlike legacy Preemptible VMs which had a fixed discount, Spot VM pricing is highly dynamic. The discount (up to 91%) fluctuates based on the current available compute capacity in a specific zone or region. For a massive 50,000 vCPU grid, capacity in a single zone will likely be exhausted, leading to high preemption rates. Distributing the load globally allows you to target zones with the lowest current Spot prices and the highest available idle capacity.

why other options are wrong.Deploy all 50,000 vCPUs in a single zone: Spot discounts are not fixed at 91%; they vary. Furthermore, requesting 50k vCPUs in one zone using Spot will almost certainly hit capacity limits and trigger massive preemptions.
why other options are wrong.Provision the grid using Preemptible VMs: Preemptible VMs are the older generation and their pricing model is being deprecated in favor of Spot VMs. Spot VMs provide deeper potential discounts and no 24-hour runtime limit.
why other options are wrong.Commit to a 3-year Flexible Committed Us: Committed Use Discounts (CUDs) cannot be applied to Spot VMs or Preemptible VMs. They are completely separate pricing mechanisms.

questions.questionText: You are running deep learning workloads on Spot VMs that require expensive initial data staging on the boot disk. If the VM is preempted, you want to avoid re-downloading the data when compute capacity becomes available again. You configure the instance's preemption action to `STOP`. Which two statements describe the behavior and billing implications of this configuration? (Choose two)
options: When preempted, the VM's state transitions to TERMINATED, but the boot disk and any attached persistent disks are retained.
While the Spot VM is stopped, you are not billed for the compute (vCPU/RAM), but you continue to incur charges for the persistent disks and static IPs.
Compute Engine will automatically restart the stopped Spot VM as soon as new spot capacity becomes available in the zone.
You must manually configure a snapshot schedule, as the STOP action deletes the persistent disk but retains an automatic snapshot for recovery.
Configuring the action to STOP allows the Spot VM to retain its attached Local SSD data across the preemption event.
correctAnswers: When preempted, the VM's state transitions to TERMINATED, but the boot disk and any attached persistent disks are retained.
While the Spot VM is stopped, you are not billed for the compute (vCPU/RAM), but you continue to incur charges for the persistent disks and static IPs.

explanation.general explanation: When a Spot VM's preemption action is set to STOP, Compute Engine shuts down the VM and changes its state to TERMINATED instead of deleting it. This preserves the boot disk and any attached persistent disks. Because the VM is not actively running, you are not billed for vCPU or memory, but you are still billed for the storage consumed by the persistent disks and any attached static IP addresses.

why other options are wrong.Compute Engine will automatically restar: Compute Engine does *not* automatically restart stopped Spot VMs. You must manually start them or use a script/MIG to attempt restarts.
why other options are wrong.You must manually configure a snapshot s: The STOP action retains the actual persistent disk, not just a snapshot. It does not delete the PD.
why other options are wrong.Configuring the action to STOP allows th: Local SSD data is always lost upon preemption, regardless of whether the preemption action is STOP or DELETE.

questions.questionText: Your organization uses a fleet of standard Compute Engine instances for an ERP system. Google Cloud schedules a disruptive host maintenance event on the underlying physical servers. To reduce costs, the CFO asks if the organization should switch the ERP system to Spot VMs. What is a critical operational difference between Standard VMs and Spot VMs during host maintenance events?
options: Standard VMs can Live Migrate transparently to new hardware, whereas Spot VMs do not support Live Migration and will be preempted (terminated/stopped) during the event.
Standard VMs are rebooted instantly, whereas Spot VMs are suspended to disk and restored automatically after the maintenance event completes.
Spot VMs receive priority over Standard VMs during Live Migration to ensure ephemeral workloads are not abruptly disrupted.
Both Standard and Spot VMs are Live Migrated, but Spot VMs will incur full standard pricing during the migration window.
correctAnswers: Standard VMs can Live Migrate transparently to new hardware, whereas Spot VMs do not support Live Migration and will be preempted (terminated/stopped) during the event.

explanation.general explanation: Live Migration is a premium feature of Standard Compute Engine VMs that allows Google to move running VMs from one physical host to another without downtime during infrastructure maintenance. Spot VMs, due to their discounted and volatile nature, do not support Live Migration. If the underlying host requires maintenance, the Spot VM is simply preempted (terminated). Therefore, running a critical ERP system on Spot VMs is an anti-pattern.

why other options are wrong.Standard VMs are rebooted instantly, whe: Spot VMs are not automatically suspended and restored by Google during maintenance; they are preempted.
why other options are wrong.Spot VMs receive priority over Standard: Spot VMs do not support Live Migration at all, let alone receive priority.

questions.questionText: You administer a GKE Standard cluster that heavily utilizes Node Auto-provisioning (NAP) to dynamically scale infrastructure based on incoming pod requirements. You deploy a new massive batch processing workload and want NAP to automatically provision Spot nodes specifically for this workload, while keeping other workloads on standard nodes. How should you configure this?
options: Configure the NAP profile globally in the GKE control plane to enable `spot-only-mode=true`.
Add the `nodeSelector` or `nodeAffinity` targeting `cloud.google.com/gke-spot=true` directly within the batch workload's Pod specification.
Create a dedicated PriorityClass named `SpotPriority` and assign it to the batch workload's deployment.
Deploy the batch workload as a Kubernetes `Job` resource, which NAP intrinsically maps to Spot instances by default.
correctAnswers: Add the `nodeSelector` or `nodeAffinity` targeting `cloud.google.com/gke-spot=true` directly within the batch workload's Pod specification.

explanation.general explanation: Node Auto-provisioning (NAP) examines pending pods and their scheduling constraints to dynamically create matching node pools. By adding a nodeSelector or nodeAffinity targeting `cloud.google.com/gke-spot=true` to your Pod specification, you explicitly signal to NAP that the pod requires a Spot node. NAP will automatically provision a Spot node pool to fulfill this request.

why other options are wrong.Configure the NAP profile globally in th: Setting this globally would force *all* newly auto-provisioned node pools to use Spot instances, violating the requirement to keep other workloads on standard nodes.
why other options are wrong.Create a dedicated PriorityClass named `: PriorityClasses are used for Pod preemption logic (which pod to evict if a node is full), not for dictating the underlying infrastructure provisioning model to NAP.
why other options are wrong.Deploy the batch workload as a Kubernete: NAP does not natively assume all `Jobs` should run on Spot instances. You must explicitly request Spot capacity via labels/selectors.

questions.questionText: Your team is migrating thousands of shell scripts that execute complex video transcoding tasks to Google Cloud Batch. To minimize costs, you configure the Cloud Batch job to execute on Spot VMs. When a Spot VM is preempted midway through a 40-minute transcoding task, what is the default behavior of Cloud Batch?
options: The specific task permanently fails, and Cloud Batch marks the overall job as 'FAILED'.
Cloud Batch automatically detects the preemption and transparently requeues the failed task to be executed on a new VM.
Cloud Batch falls back to executing the interrupted task on a Standard VM to guarantee its completion.
Cloud Batch suspends the preempted VM's memory state and instantly live-migrates the active task to another Spot VM in the pool.
correctAnswers: Cloud Batch automatically detects the preemption and transparently requeues the failed task to be executed on a new VM.

explanation.general explanation: Google Cloud Batch is fully integrated with Compute Engine's Spot provisioning model. It is designed to handle compute volatility gracefully. If a Spot VM running a Batch task is preempted, Cloud Batch automatically detects the interruption, marks the task execution as failed due to preemption, and requeues the task to be processed again on a newly provisioned instance. (Note: Because it restarts from the beginning, tasks should ideally be idempotent or implement checkpointing).

why other options are wrong.The specific task permanently fails, and: Batch is designed for fault tolerance; it retries preempted tasks based on its internal retry policies, preventing immediate job failure.
why other options are wrong.Cloud Batch falls back to executing the: Cloud Batch honors the provisioning model you specified. It does not automatically upgrade your workload to a more expensive Standard VM tier without explicit configuration.
why other options are wrong.Cloud Batch suspends the preempted VM's: Spot VMs cannot be live-migrated, and memory state is lost. The task starts fresh on the new VM.

questions.questionText: A healthcare company requires strict physical isolation for its workloads to comply with internal audits. They deploy Sole-Tenant Nodes to ensure their Compute Engine VMs do not share physical hardware with other GCP customers. To offset the high cost of sole-tenancy, they attempt to provision Spot VMs on these Sole-Tenant Nodes. What is the expected outcome?
options: The Spot VMs will provision successfully, but the discount will be capped at 30% instead of 91% due to the dedicated hardware overhead.
The provisioning request will fail, because Spot VMs and Preemptible VMs are fundamentally incompatible with Sole-Tenant Nodes.
The Spot VMs will provision successfully, but they will never be preempted because the customer exclusively owns the capacity of the node.
The provisioning request will fail unless the Sole-Tenant Node group is configured with the 'Dynamic Capacity' flag enabled.
correctAnswers: The provisioning request will fail, because Spot VMs and Preemptible VMs are fundamentally incompatible with Sole-Tenant Nodes.

explanation.general explanation: Spot VMs and legacy Preemptible VMs utilize spare, idle capacity across Google's shared multi-tenant infrastructure. Sole-Tenant Nodes provide dedicated hardware strictly for a single customer. Because the hardware is fully dedicated to you, there is no 'spare Google capacity' to utilize dynamically. Therefore, GCP strictly prohibits provisioning Spot or Preemptible VMs on Sole-Tenant Nodes.

why other options are wrong.The Spot VMs will provision successfully: Spot VMs cannot be provisioned on sole-tenant nodes at all.
Spot VMs are blocked from placement on sole-tenant nodes by design.
why other options are wrong.The provisioning request will fail unles: There is no 'Dynamic Capacity' flag for sole-tenant nodes that enables Spot VMs.

questions.questionText: You are optimizing a massive Dataproc Spark job that relies heavily on data shuffling between nodes. You configured a cluster with 5 Standard Primary workers and 45 Spot Secondary workers. During peak load, multiple Spot workers are preempted simultaneously, causing the Spark job to fail entirely due to 'FetchFailedExceptions' related to lost shuffle data. How can you architecturally resolve this while still utilizing the 45 Spot workers?
options: Enable Dataproc Enhanced Flexibility for Spark (EFS) to offload intermediate shuffle data to the Primary workers or an external system.
Switch the Primary workers to Spot VMs and the Secondary workers to Standard VMs to invert the shuffle dependency.
Implement a Dataproc Initialization Action to mount a single shared Filestore volume across all 45 Spot workers for synchronized shuffle storage.
Increase the `spark.task.maxFailures` parameter to infinity so the job retries the lost shuffle partitions indefinitely until Spot capacity returns.
correctAnswers: Enable Dataproc Enhanced Flexibility for Spark (EFS) to offload intermediate shuffle data to the Primary workers or an external system.

explanation.general explanation: In a mixed Dataproc cluster, Spot (secondary) workers perform computation but also locally store intermediate shuffle data during complex Spark operations. If a Spot node is preempted, its local shuffle data is lost, causing downstream tasks to fail (FetchFailedException). Dataproc Enhanced Flexibility for Spark (EFS) solves this by decoupling compute from shuffle storage. It configures the Spot workers to write their intermediate shuffle data to the stable Primary workers (or HDFS), ensuring that if a Spot worker dies, the shuffle data survives and the job continues smoothly.

why other options are wrong.Switch the Primary workers to Spot VMs a: This is an extreme anti-pattern. Primary workers hold HDFS data; if they are Spot VMs and get preempted, the entire cluster faces data corruption and failure.
why other options are wrong.Implement a Dataproc Initialization Acti: Using Filestore as a Spark shuffle backend is a massive performance bottleneck and highly non-standard. EFS is the native, optimized solution.
why other options are wrong.Increase the `spark.task.maxFailures` pa: While retrying helps with transient errors, indefinitely retrying massive shuffle stages wastes compute time and delays the job indefinitely. EFS solves the root cause.

questions.questionText: Your AI startup leverages Compute Engine Spot VMs with attached NVIDIA A100 GPUs for deep learning training. Recently, you have been receiving `ZONE_RESOURCE_POOL_EXHAUSTED` errors frequently, and your startup scripts fail to acquire instances. Which two architectural strategies should you implement to mitigate this specific capacity volatility while minimizing costs? (Choose two)
options: Configure the Managed Instance Group to provision resources across multiple zones within the region to increase the chance of finding available Spot GPU capacity.
Purchase a 1-year Committed Use Discount (CUD) specifically for A100 GPUs and apply it to the Spot VMs to guarantee allocation priority.
Implement fallback logic in your deployment pipeline to provision Standard VMs with A100 GPUs if the Spot VM request fails after multiple retries.
Change the preemption action of the Spot VMs from DELETE to STOP, ensuring the GPU allocation remains reserved even when the instance is preempted.
Upgrade your Cloud Billing account to Premium Support to unlock dedicated Spot capacity reserves in your preferred zone.
correctAnswers: Configure the Managed Instance Group to provision resources across multiple zones within the region to increase the chance of finding available Spot GPU capacity.
Implement fallback logic in your deployment pipeline to provision Standard VMs with A100 GPUs if the Spot VM request fails after multiple retries.

explanation.general explanation: High-end GPUs (like A100s) have extremely high demand and low spare capacity, making Spot provisioning volatile. To mitigate `ZONE_RESOURCE_POOL_EXHAUSTED` errors, you must maximize your surface area by deploying across multiple zones (or regions). Additionally, if the workload is time-sensitive, you should implement fallback logic to provision Standard (on-demand) VMs when Spot capacity is entirely unavailable, ensuring the training can proceed.

why other options are wrong.Purchase a 1-year Committed Use Discount: CUDs cannot be applied to Spot VMs. Spot VMs inherently provide no capacity guarantees, regardless of billing commitments.
why other options are wrong.Change the preemption action of the Spot: Stopping a Spot VM does not reserve the underlying hardware or GPU. The hardware is returned to the pool. When you try to start it again, you may still hit capacity errors.
why other options are wrong.Upgrade your Cloud Billing account to Pr: Spot capacity is based strictly on global idle infrastructure. Support tiers do not grant 'dedicated Spot reserves'.

questions.questionText: You are building a custom stream processing worker on a Spot VM that consumes messages from a third-party API that does not support replay. As the worker processes messages, it keeps a local SQLite database on its persistent boot disk to track which message IDs have been processed. When the Spot VM is preempted, the boot disk is deleted. How should you re-architect the state management to survive compute volatility?
options: Externalize the state by replacing the local SQLite database with a durable, managed datastore like Cloud SQL or Firestore.
Configure the Spot VM's preemption action to STOP instead of DELETE, so the SQLite database on the boot disk is preserved across preemptions.
Use a Compute Engine startup script to immediately take a snapshot of the boot disk every 60 seconds.
Mount a Regional Persistent Disk to the Spot VM so the SQLite database is synchronously replicated to a backup zone.
correctAnswers: Externalize the state by replacing the local SQLite database with a durable, managed datastore like Cloud SQL or Firestore.

explanation.general explanation: The fundamental architectural principle for designing resilient applications on volatile compute (like Spot VMs) is to decouple state from the ephemeral compute node. Writing processed message states to a local disk is an anti-pattern because the disk can be destroyed, or the VM might fail to restart. Externalizing the state to a managed, durable, highly available database (like Cloud SQL or Firestore) ensures that any replacement worker can instantly query the true, globally consistent state and resume processing.

why other options are wrong.Configure the Spot VM's preemption actio: While STOP preserves the disk, relying on a specific VM to restart to resume a streaming pipeline introduces massive latency and potential deadlocks if that specific zone remains out of capacity. Ephemeral workers should be totally replaceable.
why other options are wrong.Use a Compute Engine startup script to i: Taking snapshots every 60 seconds is highly inefficient, costly, and still leaves up to a 59-second window of data loss for non-replayable messages.
why other options are wrong.Mount a Regional Persistent Disk to the: A Regional PD ensures data survives a zone failure, but if the Spot VM is preempted and the disk is deleted (or locked by the terminated instance), it doesn't solve the architectural flaw of binding state to a volatile worker.

questions.questionText: Your Managed Instance Group (MIG) consists of 20 Spot VMs running an internal API. The MIG has an autohealer configured with an initial delay of 300 seconds and a health check interval of 10 seconds. Compute Engine suddenly preempts 5 of the Spot VMs due to a capacity spike. How does the MIG architecture respond to this specific event?
options: The autohealer detects the instances are unreachable after 10 seconds, waits for the 300-second initial delay, and then signals the MIG to recreate them.
The MIG manager intercepts the preemption signal directly from the compute infrastructure and immediately attempts to recreate the 5 instances, bypassing the autohealer logic entirely.
The MIG disables the autohealer for Spot instances by default to prevent continuous recreation loops during capacity shortages.
The autohealer marks the 5 instances as UNHEALTHY, but because they were preempted rather than crashed, the MIG waits 24 hours before attempting recreation.
correctAnswers: The MIG manager intercepts the preemption signal directly from the compute infrastructure and immediately attempts to recreate the 5 instances, bypassing the autohealer logic entirely.

explanation.general explanation: In a Managed Instance Group, preemption is an infrastructure-level event managed directly by the MIG controller. When a Spot VM is preempted, the MIG knows immediately (via internal signaling) that the VM is gone and that it must maintain the target size. It will proactively attempt to provision replacement instances. The autohealer is an application-level mechanism (checking if an HTTP endpoint responds) and is bypassed completely during a preemption event.

why other options are wrong.The autohealer detects the instances are: The autohealer is irrelevant for preemptions. Preemptions are recognized directly by the infrastructure. (Also, initial delay applies to *newly* created instances, not existing ones failing).
why other options are wrong.The MIG disables the autohealer for Spot: Autohealers are fully supported and highly recommended on Spot MIGs to catch application crashes, independent of preemptions.
why other options are wrong.The autohealer marks the 5 instances as: The MIG actively and continuously attempts to recreate preempted instances to meet its target size; it does not wait 24 hours.

questions.questionText: You configured a Managed Instance Group containing Spot VMs behind a Global External Application Load Balancer. To ensure smooth scaling, you configured Connection Draining on the backend service with a timeout of 300 seconds (5 minutes). If Compute Engine decides to preempt one of the active Spot VMs, how will the load balancer and the instance interact regarding active client connections? (Choose two)
options: The Load Balancer will immediately stop sending new requests to the preempted instance upon receiving the preemption signal.
The Spot VM will honor the 300-second connection draining timeout and remain active until all existing connections successfully close.
The Load Balancer will forcefully sever any remaining active connections to the instance after exactly 30 seconds.
Compute Engine will suspend the instance's preemption process until the Load Balancer signals that connection draining is complete.
The Spot VM will automatically migrate the active TCP connections to another healthy instance in the MIG.
correctAnswers: The Load Balancer will immediately stop sending new requests to the preempted instance upon receiving the preemption signal.
The Load Balancer will forcefully sever any remaining active connections to the instance after exactly 30 seconds.

explanation.general explanation: Connection draining allows existing connections to complete when an instance is removed from a load balancer. However, Spot VMs have a strict, unchangeable 30-second preemption warning. When preemption occurs, the instance is removed from the backend, so new requests stop. Even though connection draining is set to 300 seconds, the hardware disappears after 30 seconds. Therefore, the load balancer will sever any active connections that haven't finished within that 30-second window, overriding the 300-second draining configuration.

why other options are wrong.The Spot VM will honor the 300-second co: Hardware limits (30s preemption) override software configurations (300s draining). The VM physically cannot remain active.
why other options are wrong.Compute Engine will suspend the instance: Preemption is driven by Google's global capacity needs and cannot be delayed by customer application load balancers.
why other options are wrong.The Spot VM will automatically migrate t: TCP connections cannot be seamlessly migrated between distinct VMs in this architecture.

questions.questionText: Your team is migrating a highly available MongoDB replica set to GKE using StatefulSets. The cluster must survive node failures. A DevOps engineer suggests provisioning the GKE node pool using Spot instances to reduce the database hosting costs by up to 90%. Why must you reject this configuration?
options: StatefulSets are incompatible with the `pd.csi.storage.gke.io` provisioner on Spot instances.
Spot instances cannot be attached to internal VPC networks, preventing the MongoDB replicas from communicating.
Simultaneous preemption of multiple Spot nodes can cause the replica set to lose quorum, resulting in immediate database unavailability and potential data corruption.
GKE automatically forces pods on Spot nodes to be stateless by mounting `/data` as an ephemeral `emptyDir` volume.
correctAnswers: Simultaneous preemption of multiple Spot nodes can cause the replica set to lose quorum, resulting in immediate database unavailability and potential data corruption.

explanation.general explanation: Spot VMs are highly volatile and can be preempted at any time, often simultaneously if a region experiences a capacity crunch. Stateful clustered databases (like MongoDB, Cassandra, ZooKeeper) rely on maintaining a quorum of active nodes to accept writes and ensure consistency. If multiple Spot nodes are preempted at once, the database loses quorum, goes offline, and might suffer split-brain or data corruption scenarios. Spot nodes are strictly an anti-pattern for core stateful database workloads.

why other options are wrong.StatefulSets are incompatible with the `: StatefulSets and Persistent Volumes work perfectly fine on Spot nodes technically, the issue is architectural resilience, not technical incompatibility.
why other options are wrong.Spot instances cannot be attached to int: Spot instances have standard VPC networking capabilities.
why other options are wrong.GKE automatically forces pods on Spot no: GKE does not alter pod volume mounts based on the node's provisioning model. If you specify a PersistentVolumeClaim, GKE will mount a PD.

questions.questionText: A finance director is reviewing the billing impact of adopting Spot VMs for the company's non-production environments. They notice that the discount applied to the Spot VMs varies wildly between different days and regions, sometimes offering 60% savings and other times 90%. What governs the dynamic pricing mechanism of Spot VMs on Google Cloud?
options: The pricing is dynamically adjusted based on the aggregate spot capacity demanded by the customer's specific billing account.
The pricing fluctuates dynamically based on real-time supply and demand of unallocated compute capacity in a specific zone and machine type.
The pricing is determined by the `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` specified in the instance template; shorter grace periods yield steeper discounts.
The pricing varies based on the amount of Committed Use Discounts (CUDs) the organization has purchased globally.
correctAnswers: The pricing fluctuates dynamically based on real-time supply and demand of unallocated compute capacity in a specific zone and machine type.

explanation.general explanation: Spot VM pricing is a market-driven model designed to sell Google's excess, idle infrastructure capacity. The price dynamically fluctuates (up to a 91% discount off standard on-demand pricing) based on the real-time supply and demand for specific machine types within specific zones. When demand is low and idle capacity is high, the discount is deep. When capacity tightens, the price rises (and preemptions occur).

why other options are wrong.The pricing is dynamically adjusted base: Pricing is based on global multi-tenant supply/demand, not isolated to a single customer's account usage.
why other options are wrong.The pricing is determined by the `termin: The preemption warning is fixed at 30 seconds for Spot VMs; there is no configurable grace period that alters the price.
why other options are wrong.The pricing varies based on the amount o: CUDs and Spot pricing are entirely separate mechanisms. Purchasing CUDs does not affect your Spot discount rate.

questions.questionText: You are automating the deployment of a new Spot VM backend using Terraform (`google_compute_instance_template`). You must correctly configure the instance template to utilize the Spot provisioning model and handle preemptions gracefully by stopping the instances. Which two configurations must be explicitly defined in the `scheduling` block? (Choose two)
options: Set `provisioning_model` to `"SPOT"`.
Set `instance_termination_action` to `"STOP"`.
Set `on_host_maintenance` to `"MIGRATE"`.
Set `preemptible` to `false` to explicitly differentiate it from legacy models.
Set `automatic_restart` to `true` to ensure the instance recovers quickly.
correctAnswers: Set `provisioning_model` to `"SPOT"`.
Set `instance_termination_action` to `"STOP"`.

explanation.general explanation: To configure an instance template for Spot VMs via Terraform or API, you must specify the `provisioning_model` as `"SPOT"`. To ensure the instances are stopped rather than deleted upon preemption, you must set the `instance_termination_action` to `"STOP"`. Note that for Spot VMs, `preemptible` must generally be set to `true` (or omitted as it defaults based on model), `on_host_maintenance` must be `TERMINATE`, and `automatic_restart` must be `false`.

why other options are wrong.Set `on_host_maintenance` to `\"MIGRATE\: Spot VMs do not support live migration. This must be set to `TERMINATE`.
why other options are wrong.Set `preemptible` to `false` to explicit: Spot VMs are a type of preemptible VM. Setting this to false conflicts with the SPOT provisioning model.
why other options are wrong.Set `automatic_restart` to `true` to ens: Spot VMs cannot use automatic_restart. If they are preempted, the infrastructure does not restart them automatically (unless managed by a MIG).

questions.questionText: A media rendering pipeline uses a high-throughput Cloud Filestore instance to store massive raw video files. A pool of 100 Spot VMs mounts the Filestore volume, renders the frames, and writes the output back to the volume. Which statement accurately describes the architectural interaction between compute volatility and the Filestore storage allocation?
options: Because Spot VMs are ephemeral, Cloud Filestore forces the NFS mount to be strictly read-only to prevent data corruption during preemptions.
If a Spot VM is preempted mid-write, the Filestore volume might contain partially written files, requiring the application pipeline to handle file cleanup or overwrite logic.
Compute Engine intelligently flushes all pending NFS I/O operations to Filestore automatically when the 30-second preemption signal is sent.
Spot VMs cannot mount Cloud Filestore because NFS requires persistent IP reservations which are dropped upon preemption.
correctAnswers: If a Spot VM is preempted mid-write, the Filestore volume might contain partially written files, requiring the application pipeline to handle file cleanup or overwrite logic.

explanation.general explanation: Spot VMs are fully capable of mounting Cloud Filestore (NFS) in read-write mode. However, if a Spot VM is preempted abruptly while writing a file, the NFS connection drops. The file on Filestore will be partially written. The underlying infrastructure does not automatically clean up these application-level files. The media pipeline architecture must be robust enough to detect incomplete tasks and overwrite or delete partially rendered frames when another worker picks up the job.

why other options are wrong.Because Spot VMs are ephemeral, Cloud Fi: Filestore allows ReadWriteMany access regardless of the compute provisioning model.
why other options are wrong.Compute Engine intelligently flushes all: The OS does not guarantee flushing of application buffers to network storage automatically upon receiving an ACPI signal. You must handle this in a shutdown script.
why other options are wrong.Spot VMs cannot mount Cloud Filestore be: Spot VMs receive standard internal IPs within the VPC and can perfectly mount Filestore.

questions.questionText: Your operations team runs a large fleet of Spot VMs. They want to proactively trigger an alert when the global availability of Spot capacity in your chosen region tightens, specifically when the preemption rate exceeds 15% of your fleet within a 1-hour window. How should you instrument this observability?
options: Create a log-based metric counting the 'GCE_VM_PREEMPTION' audit logs, and build an alerting policy dividing this by the total active instance count.
Use Cloud Monitoring to create an Alerting Policy based on the `compute.googleapis.com/instance/preemptions` metric and track its rate of increase.
Configure the MIG Autoscaler to push its internal `SpotCapacityError` events to a Pub/Sub topic linked to Cloud Functions for alerting.
Monitor the `compute.googleapis.com/instance/uptime` metric; any VM with an uptime under 1 hour triggers a preemption alert.
correctAnswers: Use Cloud Monitoring to create an Alerting Policy based on the `compute.googleapis.com/instance/preemptions` metric and track its rate of increase.

explanation.general explanation: Google Cloud provides a native, dedicated Cloud Monitoring metric specifically for tracking Spot/Preemptible VM preemptions: `compute.googleapis.com/instance/preemptions`. By creating an alerting policy based on the rate of this metric relative to your fleet size, you can effectively monitor capacity tightening and operational disruption.

why other options are wrong.Create a log-based metric counting the ': While preemptions generate audit logs, building custom log-based metrics is unnecessary and less efficient than using the native, pre-calculated `instance/preemptions` metric.
why other options are wrong.Configure the MIG Autoscaler to push its: This is overly complex and does not directly measure the preemption rate of running instances, only the failure to provision new ones.
why other options are wrong.Monitor the `compute.googleapis.com/inst: Instances can have low uptime for many reasons (autoscaling scale-up, manual restarts, deployments). This does not accurately track preemptions.

questions.questionText: An enterprise is designing a 'Pilot Light' disaster recovery architecture in a secondary GCP region (`us-west1`). To minimize the continuous running costs, a junior architect proposes running the core foundational infrastructure (Active Directory domain controller replica and database asynchronous replica) on Spot VMs. What is the fundamental architectural flaw in this design?
options: Spot VMs cannot establish cross-region VPN or Interconnect connections required for data replication.
During a primary region disaster, traffic will spike in `us-west1`, causing Google to immediately preempt all Spot VMs to preserve bandwidth.
Spot VMs do not support asynchronous disk replication across regions.
Core infrastructure must be highly available. If the Spot VMs are preempted right before or during an actual disaster, the DR capability is completely broken.
correctAnswers: Core infrastructure must be highly available. If the Spot VMs are preempted right before or during an actual disaster, the DR capability is completely broken.

explanation.general explanation: A 'Pilot Light' DR strategy maintains a minimal, always-on core infrastructure (like AD and DB replicas) that allows you to rapidly scale up application servers when a disaster hits. These core components must be rock-solid and highly available. If they are run on Spot VMs, they could be preempted at any moment. If a disaster occurs while your Pilot Light Spot VMs are preempted, your entire DR strategy fails. Spot VMs are strictly an anti-pattern for foundational DR infrastructure.

why other options are wrong.Spot VMs cannot establish cross-region V: Spot VMs have full networking capabilities and can use Cloud VPN/Interconnect.
why other options are wrong.During a primary region disaster, traffi: Spot preemption is based on compute capacity supply/demand, not network traffic spikes.
why other options are wrong.Spot VMs do not support asynchronous dis: PD Asynchronous Replication is supported on disks attached to Spot VMs (though functionally useless if the VM is volatile).

questions.questionText: You are deploying a microservices application on GKE containing a 'Checkout' service (processes payments, highly sensitive to latency/drops) and an 'Analytics' service (processes clickstreams asynchronously, highly fault-tolerant). You want to optimize the cluster for both cost and reliability. How should you segregate the workload placement?
options: Deploy both services in a single Spot node pool. Add a `PreemptionPriority: High` label to the Checkout pod so GKE preempts the Analytics pods first when capacity tightens.
Deploy both services on a Standard node pool, but configure the Analytics service to use Local SSDs to offset the compute cost.
Create two node pools: a Standard node pool and a Spot node pool. Use `nodeAffinity` to schedule the Checkout service on Standard nodes, and the Analytics service on Spot nodes.
Use a Regional cluster and deploy the Checkout service to the primary zone on Standard nodes, and the Analytics service to the secondary zone on Spot nodes.
correctAnswers: Create two node pools: a Standard node pool and a Spot node pool. Use `nodeAffinity` to schedule the Checkout service on Standard nodes, and the Analytics service on Spot nodes.

explanation.general explanation: The standard architectural pattern for mixed reliability requirements in GKE is to use multiple node pools. The mission-critical 'Checkout' service must run on stable, Standard nodes to ensure payments are never dropped due to infrastructure volatility. The asynchronous, fault-tolerant 'Analytics' service is a perfect fit for Spot nodes to save costs. `nodeAffinity` or `nodeSelector` is used to enforce this scheduling segregation.

why other options are wrong.Deploy both services in a single Spot no: Preemption logic is dictated by Google Cloud infrastructure, not Kubernetes priority labels. If the node is preempted, ALL pods on it are killed, regardless of priority.
why other options are wrong.Deploy both services on a Standard node: Local SSDs actually increase infrastructure costs, they do not offset compute costs.
why other options are wrong.Use a Regional cluster and deploy the Ch: GKE node pools automatically span all zones in a regional cluster. You segregate by node pool, not by forcing services into specific physical zones manually just for volatility routing.
